text:
Marathon Petroleum closed up 1.1% today, but that modest gain masks a brutal two-week slide of 9.1% — and today's bounce came despite headwinds that hammered refinery stocks yesterday. The core problem: refining margins are shrinking, even as crude oil prices climbed on Middle East conflict concerns. When a refiner's profit per barrel (the gap between what it pays for crude and what it sells gasoline and diesel for) gets thinner, the stock tends to fall, which is exactly what happened on October 27th when the stock dropped $34.66. Today's small rebound appears to be a technical bounce rather than a fix to the underlying issue.

The broader squeeze is visible in the numbers: gasoline and diesel inventories remain elevated at 209 and 103 million barrels respectively, while refineries are humming at 92.8% capacity. That flood of supply — combined with talk of additional Russian diesel entering the market — is pushing fuel prices lower even though crude costs remain high at $103 per barrel. For a refinery operator, that's the worst scenario: high input costs meeting weak output prices.
